name: Strongyloides stercoralis

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Rhabditiform larva: roughly 180–380 µm, short buccal cavity and prominent genital primordium.
Filariform larva: up to about 600 µm, long esophagus and notched tail; eggs usually hatch before passage and are not the usual stool target.

transmission.detail: Soil-derived L3 enter skin; intestinal females produce offspring that may exit or initiate autoinfection. A free-living generation can occur outside the host.

life_cycle.detail: Larvae develop through direct or free-living pathways.
Parasitic females produce eggs that hatch.
Larvae leave in stool or participate in autoinfection.

hosts: Parasitic definitive host: humans; animal-associated lineages also occur. No intermediate host.
distribution: Tropical and subtropical regions including Southeast Asia; persistent infection may remain after leaving an endemic area.
clinical_significance: Can cause abdominal symptoms, diarrhea and skin manifestations; immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids, can precipitate hyperinfection or dissemination.
specimen: Rhabditiform larvae in stool; larvae in respiratory material may occur in hyperinfection.
diagnostics: Stool larval concentration, Baermann or agar-plate methods in equipped laboratories; serology or molecular testing can complement microscopy.
differential_diagnosis: Hookworm rhabditiform larvae have a longer buccal cavity and less conspicuous genital primordium. A cropped midbody alone is insufficient.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated
description: Strongyloides stercoralis — Intestinal threadworm. Can cause abdominal symptoms, diarrhea and skin manifestations; immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids, can precipitate hyperinfection or dissemination.

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
